scenario: AITA for telling my teacher 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!' | 20, almost 21, f. taking my first semester of uni since i can finally afford it. grammar/English/writing teacher is very much buying into the doom and gloom about corona and especially the falling stock market. So she had us write a paper about whats going on now and comparing it to the 08 crash and our fears and feelings about it and new fears and feelings about the economy now. Thing is... 08 and 09 were AWESOME for me. My little 9ish year old self had a fun couple of years. Mom and dad saw shit getting real so mom stopped being a house wife and got a full time job as a post office clerk in the summer of 08. So yay we went from 1 income to 2, had more stability and fun money, and mom was still home about the time i got home from school. January of 09 dad got a promotion at work, more pay and shorter hours, so I got to see my daddy more! And again the household income went up. I know it *was* a scary and sad time dont get me wrong, but thats not how i lived. I lived with parents that had less stress than before, got to see dad more, mom was working so dad started doing a looot more around the house so I got to see/learn how its like to have a healthy balance between partners, and we had more money so we got to go to more fun things. Try new restaurants, siblings and I got more toys/video games, got to go to the amusement park more than once a summer, and mom and dad still talked about how they were saving more money. So yeah... good times. Now, well my fiance just got his masters degree in CS, and a promotion at his job due to it, and is helping me through uni with money to spare. Yeah, you can see where this is going. Things are headed up again. So thats what I put in my paper. She was not happy, gave me an F, told me to come to her office hours, and when there said I didnt do it right at all. She said she wanted my fears and worries not for me to brag about how great life is for me and me alone. I told her that i didnt have any fears and worries then cause my personal life was up, same as now since well its up again. she tried to berate me some more about honesty and accountability in writing, when i stopped her and told her 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!'. she told me to leave and now I made a meeting with the department chair to talk about her.

Here’s a balanced perspective to consider: ### **Potential Benefits:** 1. **Unity & Tradition** – If the wedding has a strong family tradition of coordinated outfits (e.g., bridesmaids, groomsmen, or even extended family), it can feel meaningful and symbolic. 2. **Photography** – Matching fabrics can create cohesive, visually striking photos, especially if everyone is wearing complementary colors or patterns. 3. **Ease of Coordination** – If you’re not great at matching outfits, this ensures everyone looks intentional and put-together. 4. **Sentimental Value** – Some families cherish the idea of "matching" as a way to honor the couple or create a shared memory. ### **Potential Drawbacks:** 1. **Cost** – Buying fabric (especially high-quality or custom-made) can be expensive, especially if multiple people are involved. Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. (Next Steps)** 1. **Apologize to the Teacher (If You Want to Keep the Door Open)** - You don’t owe her an apology for your **original feelings**, but if you want to **rebuild trust** (for future classes, references, etc.), a **short, sincere message** could help: > *"I realize now that my response was unprofessional, and I regret saying what I did. I still believe my paper was fair, but I understand why you were upset. I’ll keep that in mind moving forward."* 2. **Prepare for the Department Chair Meeting** - **Bring copies** of: - Your original paper. - Her feedback. - Any emails/conversations about the grade. - **Focus on**: - The **grade was unfair** (you met the assignment’s requirements). - The **teacher’s expectations were unclear** (she wanted "fears," but you provided a valid personal perspective). - **Avoid** bringing up the "bitch" comment unless she brings it up—**let the grade be the issue, not your tone**. 3. **Reflect on the Larger Issue** - This situation highlights a **bigger problem**: **Academia often expects students to adopt a single narrative** (even if it doesn’t match their reality). - **Question**: *Should you even be in a class where the teacher’s worldview feels so dismissive of your experience?* - If this is a **required class**, suck it up and focus on the grade. - If it’s **elective**, consider whether this professor’s teaching style aligns with your values. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It AITA?** **Yes, in the short term.** Your reaction was **understandable as a moment of frustration**, but it **damaged your academic standing** and **closed doors** that could’ve been opened with a more strategic approach. **No, if you consider intent.** You were **being honest** about your experience, and her reaction was **unfair**. But **honesty ≠ entitlement**, and academia (like many institutions) **rewards compliance over rebellion**. --- ### **What You Can Take Away** 1. **Your truth matters**, but **so does your future**. 2. **Anger is valid**, but **impulsive outbursts often backfire**. 3. **Academia is a power structure**—even if you disagree with a teacher, **escalating poorly can hurt you more than them**. 4. **This might be a wake-up call** about whether this environment is right for you long-term.
